paragraphs.en: The bus [[left|leave]] me at the edge of a small [[village]] in [[Virginia]] just after noon, and the [[glare]] off the asphalt was fierce enough to make me shade my eyes.
My [[granny]] was waiting by the gate, small and straight-backed, with the same [[vigor]] she had when I was a boy.
A [[heavy]] smell of [[orange]] peel and hot dust filled her kitchen, where an old [[fan]] turned slowly above the table.
I had come for the summer to help restore the old [[theatre]] on the hill, a building that seemed to [[belong]] to another [[era]].
It was, [[undoubtedly]], the strangest summer of my life.
Granny still [[reaped|reap]] a [[crop]] of [[cucumbers|cucumber]] from the strip of soil behind the [[hedge]] and refused any [[help]] with the watering.
But a [[cataract]] had clouded her right eye, and the [[surgeon]] in the county town warned that waiting too [[long]] would make the operation harder.
Her [[inability]] to read the small [[text]] in the paper [[annoyed|annoy]] her more than the pain did, because reading had always been her quiet [[pastime]].
She would [[not]] admit [[fear]], though a [[feeble]] lamp above the stairs showed how fast her sight was going.
A short [[nod]] was her way of ending such conversations, so I stopped arguing and began to [[search]] for a [[cure]] that did not depend on her stubbornness.
The theatre had a [[majestic]] [[dome]] and a [[superhigh]] arch above the stage, and its windows let in a dusty gold light.
The walls still carried the names of local [[nobility]] and a faded portrait of a [[queen]] in a [[golden]] frame.
In the loft waited a pipe [[organ]], and on the stage a [[virtuoso]] had once played until the whole hall seemed to [[glow]].
Behind the stage was a [[suite]] of dressing rooms, each with a cracked [[mirror]], a wooden [[bench]], and a [[noisy]] door.
A [[patch]] of damp had spread across the ceiling, and the floorboards rose at a [[bend]] near the [[position]] of the old lighting [[device]].
I [[recall]] standing there that first afternoon, feeling a [[surge]] of [[emotion]] I could not name.
On Monday the committee met under the dome to divide a small [[surplus]] of [[capital]].
There was [[no]] agreement on the [[quota]] of free seats for old people, and [[not]] one member trusted the [[parity]] between town and county money.
A [[consulting]] firm had sent a report whose [[criteria]] were written for a city, not for a valley.
Mr. Hale, a [[well-meaning]] farmer with a [[superior]] manner, wanted to spend [[everything]] on a [[mass-market]] estate at the edge of the meadow.
His plan would drain the [[ditch]], cut the [[hedge]], and damage the [[ecosystem]] that kept the stream clear.
Most of us preferred [[voluntary]] labour and better [[accessibility]] for wheelchairs to any [[whopping]] new building.
Hale's smile was [[insincere]], and his speech was [[self-serving]] from the first sentence to the last.
On Saturday the village held its annual [[cricket]] match, the one [[pastime]] that still brought every generation to the same field.
I had never [[tried|try]] the game before, and my [[opponent]] was a boy of twelve with a [[superb]] eye.
He [[caught|catch]] two hard balls at the boundary, and a [[crow]] on the fence watched him as if it knew the [[score]].
The match stayed close until the last over, when a [[well-known]] teacher hit the ball into the [[ditch]] and ran [[headlong]] between the wickets.
I dropped an easy catch, and my [[self-esteem]] sank until Granny, watching from a [[bench]], said I had [[acted|act]] with more [[passion]] than skill.
It was a [[pleasurable]] afternoon, and for a few hours nobody mentioned the developer or the [[crisis]].
The fair on Sunday filled the green with a [[cate]] tent, a [[textile]] stall, and the smell of fried bread.
Every [[commodity]] on the tables carried a handwritten [[sticker]] with its price.
A [[symbolic]] ribbon was cut by the oldest woman in the village, and two men began to [[assemble]] a [[patchwork]] quilt on the grass.
I bought a [[little]] bowl for Granny and, [[besides]] that, a jar of honey for the committee.
[[Beside]] the gate a neighbour asked, in a [[whisper]], whether the theatre would really reopen.
The [[theft]] was discovered on Tuesday: the [[crown]] from the costume room, fake but [[golden]], had vanished.
The [[investigation]] began with a [[hint]] from a child who had seen a stranger near the [[runway]] of the county airfield.
The police could find no [[fault]] in our locks, and the case went to the [[court]] in the county town.
I had to [[testify]], and the [[criminal]] turned out to be a man who had once repaired the roof.
A reporter got a [[scoop]] and put the story on the front page under a [[headline]] about the missing crown; the whole business felt like a [[nightmare]].
On Thursday I drove Granny to the city, where the [[surgeon]] was a calm woman with a [[mastery]] of small jokes.
The operation took less than an hour, and the [[cure]] was so quick that Granny asked whether the doctors had done anything at all.
In the waiting room I felt a [[surge]] of [[gloom]], then saw a [[gleam]] of hope when the nurse smiled.
Her [[feeble]] voice on the phone had frightened me, but her [[vigour]] returned before evening.
She said the city was too [[noisy]] and announced that she would [[leave]] the next morning.
The developer's letters did not [[imply]] a threat, yet they made the valley's [[fate]] clear: the meadow would be sold by Christmas.
The plan was put to the [[test]] at a public meeting, where an [[eminent]] lawyer explained what the [[decrease]] in young families meant for the school.
His report was [[unfavorable]] to the developer in one county and [[unfavourable]] in another, which only showed how [[unreasonable]] the rules had become.
Granny asked him to do her a [[favor]] and read the [[oral]] history of the valley aloud, and he was clearly in [[favour]] of the idea.
In the [[past]] such meetings had ended with a [[noble]] promise and no money, and I had no [[reason]] to expect better.
Still, the hall was full, and that fact alone gave me a [[positive]] feeling.
We set the work in [[order]]: wood, wiring, seats, paint, one [[category]] per week.
The wiring was [[time-consuming]], and my own [[laziness]] on the first Monday cost us a day.
I sent an [[e-mail]] to the heritage office and a longer [[email]] to an architect who had worked on old [[theaters|theater]].
The bank would not [[lend]] us money without a [[sure]] guarantee, so we asked the state [[senate]] for a [[supplement]] to the county grant.
A small [[cult]] had grown around the old building, and students came from the city to [[improve]] the garden in their [[leisure]] hours.
For a week the restoration was the [[headline]] in the county paper, and I learned to [[master]] the lighting board.
The [[secret]] of the theatre's survival, I began to see, was not money but the [[mindset]] of people who refused to [[go]] quietly.
An [[improper]] shortcut in the accounts nearly ruined us, and the [[unfairness]] of the county [[quota]] made the [[surplus]] look like a joke.
We treated every dollar with [[caution]], and the treasurer wrote each payment in a small notebook.
To my [[surprise]], a retired builder offered to [[do]] the roof himself and would take no payment.
I could only [[glimpse]] the scale of the work, and it was [[impossible]] to [[undo]] the years of neglect in one [[season]].
Some evenings I sat on the steps and felt the [[blur]] of weeks pass like a single day.
Opening night came at the [[height]] of summer, with a [[glow]] of lamps along the road.
A [[well-known]] quartet played a [[masterpiece]] by a local composer, and the sound seemed to [[surpass]] anything I had heard in a concert hall.
The old play had been a [[bestseller]] in English and a [[best-seller]] in French, though nobody could explain why.
The audience [[crushed|crush]] toward the door, and I heard a [[whisper]] that the portrait had been cleaned at last.
The new lights seemed to [[complement]] the carved wood, and the whole building [[impressed|impress]] even the sceptics.
Granny sat in the front row, her [[frown]] gone, and I wanted to [[thank]] her for making me stay.
In that [[whirl]] of applause I understood what [[culture]] means in a place that has almost nothing else.
The developer withdrew in September, and my granny called the vote a [[massacre]] of common sense.
His lawyer argued that the village had no [[option]] but to sell, yet the meadow stayed green.
The [[cause]] of our victory was simple: we had [[support]] from every [[sector]] of village life.
Donations arrived in a steady [[supply]], and a [[globe]] in the schoolroom was repainted as a thank-you to the children who had raised money.
I had to [[cross]] the field each morning to collect the post, pushing a bicycle whose [[wheel]] had lost its shape.
The wind would [[whip]] the flag on the dome, and I would [[forget]], for a moment, that I had ever lived anywhere else.
A [[superstition]] among the older actors said the theatre would close again if anyone whistled backstage, so we never did.
By October the boy from the cricket match had become a local [[superstar]], and even the county paper interviewed him.
I tried to [[extract]] one lesson from the summer, though the answer [[probably]] depended on whom you asked.
Granny said the village had [[passed|pass]] from fear to pride without ever admitting it.
[[Socially]], the theatre had become the centre of the village, and its stage was never empty for long.
The old [[unfashionable]] belief that a small place can look after itself turned out to be true, though only because many people were [[active]].
I had to [[curb]] my urge to stay, pack my bag, and return to the city.
But I knew I would come back, and the thought made me [[cry]] for the first time all summer.
The whole summer stayed in me like an [[ember]] that refused to go out.
